subject: No shopkeeper. No CCTV. Now ₹870 Cr.
preview_text: The Bengaluru batter brand that trusted its customers first.
headline: No shopkeeper. No CCTV. Now ₹870 Cr.
cover_alt: 90 to 95% of the money came back when iD Fresh let Bengaluru pay on trust, the company said in 2016.
lead_before_diagram: iD Fresh Food is the Bengaluru company behind the idli and dosa batter in your fridge. Its FY26 numbers came out this week. Operating revenue rose 27.7% to ₹870 Cr, from ₹681 Cr. Profit before tax and exceptional items went from ₹24 Cr to ₹79 Cr.

One note on that profit. The accounts also carry about ₹713 Cr of exceptional items, mostly accounting adjustments and a gain from deconsolidating a subsidiary. So ₹79 Cr is the cleaner number to watch.
Now think about what iD asks of a family. Hand your breakfast to a factory. Believe a packet when it says there are no preservatives. That's a hard sell, and the company knew it.
Back in 2016, its marketing manager told The News Minute: "We could sense consumer skepticism over our claim." So iD did something that sounds like a bad idea.
diagram_alt: Three customer doubts mapped to what iD Fresh did in 2016. Is it really fresh? Refilled every day, at apartment gates. Does this brand trust me? No staff, no CCTV, pay into a box. Do people actually pay? 90 to 95% of the money came back, the company said.
lead_after_diagram: In late April 2016, iD put small fridges at apartment entrances in 17 locations around Bengaluru. One stood at the gate of an apartment in Domlur. Batter, parathas and chapatis inside. No one manning it. No CCTV. You took what you wanted and dropped the money into a small locker fitted to the fridge. The fridges were refilled every day.

The company said 90 to 95% of the money came back. On some days it was more than 100%, as people paid extra or settled up for earlier purchases. That's iD's own figure, and it's ten years old. But look at what the setup said without a single ad: we trust you, and our food doesn't last long enough to sit around, so we restock it daily, right where you live.

Most brands try to earn trust by claiming it. "Trusted by thousands." "100% natural." Customers have read those lines so often they no longer register. iD went first. It extended trust to the customer, in public, and let the result become the story.

Ten years on, the brand is closing in on ₹900 Cr in revenue. The trust shops weren't the whole reason. Product, distribution and years of execution did most of the work. But the shops gave a claim people doubted something solid to stand on.
section_title: What this means for your brand
section_intro: You don't need fridges at apartment gates. But if customers doubt one thing you say, the fix is rarely saying it louder. Three things worth doing this week:

steps.title: Name the claim people doubt.
steps.body: Fresh, safe, on time, genuine. Pick the one customers question most. If you're not sure, read your last twenty sales objections.

steps.title: Find a way to go first.
steps.body: Pay after delivery, a free first order, a no-questions refund. Choose one policy that trusts the customer before they've proved anything.

steps.title: Put it where the decision happens.
steps.body: iD put its proof at the apartment gate, not on a website. Put yours on the homepage, in the proposal, at the counter. A policy nobody sees earns nothing.

closer: Claiming trust costs nothing. That's why nobody believes it. Risk some.

short_takes.name: GIVA, Bengaluru
short_takes.body: The jewellery brand started online in 2019. It just raised ₹975 Cr, led by Multiples, a mix of primary and secondary capital. FY26 revenue was ₹865 Cr, up from ₹505 Cr, per its CEO, and it expects to turn profitable in FY28. Much of the money goes into shops: 160 more on top of about 425. Offline orders are worth nearly twice online ones. At higher prices, a counter you can walk back to does the selling.

short_takes.name: Cent, Bengaluru
short_takes.body: Cent asks healthy people to pay for a full-body scan before anything feels wrong. Its annual check starts at ₹23,500. The company says it has done 10,000 scans, and it just raised $15 million led by Blume Ventures and South Park Commons. It also says specialists review every finding its AI flags. When customers can't judge the product themselves, show them the person checking it. That line does more than any feature list.
